**In Praise of Wandering**

Someone has just handed me a blank page, or its digital equivalent, and said, write freely about whatever you want, for a long time, without a topic assigned and without a destination in mind. I am supposed to treat this as freedom. And it is freedom, I think, but it is also the strangely specific kind of freedom that only arrives when you are told in advance that you may go anywhere. It is the freedom of someone standing at a crossroads with a sign that says *Anywhere*, pointing in every direction at once. At first I want to be sensible and choose one road cleanly and follow it to its proper end, to deliver a thesis and then supporting evidence like a responsible traveler with an itinerary. But the instruction is to write freely, and so perhaps the first free act is to refuse to be sensible in that way, to allow the thought to wander out of the gate and see where the path actually leads, even if it doubles back, even if it ends up in an unrelated field, even if I forget for a while why I set out at all.

I remember, for no good reason, a field behind the house where I grew up. It was not a remarkable field. It was not particularly pretty, and it appeared on no postcard, but in summer it had tall grass and a ditch that ran crookedly along one side and a few trees that no one had planted on purpose and that nobody bothered to cut down. I went there almost every day for a stretch of years, not to do anything in particular, which was the whole point. I would walk a circuit that was never exactly the same circuit twice, because I would be distracted by a beetle, or by the exact blue of the sky at four o'clock, or by a sudden thought about whether the ditch water reached the river by a path I could follow on foot. The field taught me a lesson that school, with its bells and its right answers, rarely did: that a place can be known intimately without ever being mastered, and that familiarity is not the same as having a map of it.

There is a difference, I have come to believe, between getting lost and being lost. Being lost is a condition, usually an unpleasant one, in which you do not know where you are and you very much want to know. Getting lost is an activity, often a deliberate one, in which you suspend that desire for a while and let yourself be guided by curiosity rather than need. Children do it instinctively. They follow a butterfly into a bramble patch and emerge scratched and delighted, having discovered that the bramble patch connects, by a secret tunnel of grass, to the garden wall. Adults do it less often, and when we do, we tend to apologize for it. We say we took a wrong turn. We say we got distracted. We rarely say, with pride, that we went the long way because the light was falling through the trees in a way that made the whole street look briefly sacred, and we wanted more of it.

Maps are the great enemy and the great ally of this kind of wandering. A map is a beautiful act of compression, an attempt to persuade the world to hold still long enough to be useful. The best maps admit, in their spare lines and careful legends, that they are lying by telling the truth, that they have left out a thousand things in order to show the few things that matter for a particular purpose. The worst maps pretend they have left nothing out, and they lead you confidently into a cul-de-sac that the mapmaker never visited. I have always loved the old maps most, the ones with sea monsters in the uncharted oceans and with cartouches in the corners where artists drew allegories of the winds. Those errors are honest in a way that a perfect satellite image is not. They say: we were here, we did not know, and so we imagined, and our imagination was made of the stories we had heard from sailors who were themselves probably lost.

If you look at the history of mapmaking, it is a history of wandering made respectable after the fact. Someone walked a coastline he had no business walking, made notes in a damp notebook, argued with the natives about the names of things, got sick, maybe got shipwrecked, and then, years later, someone else sat in a quiet room and drew a clean line for where he had stumbled. The clean line is useful. We all need clean lines to get to the airport. But we should not confuse the clean line with the walking. The walking was slower, wetter, more confused, and more alive. Every route we take today, every blue line on a phone screen that tells us to turn left in two hundred feet, is the ghost of someone's wandering, tidied up and stripped of its uncertainty.

Rivers understand this better than roads do. A road is an argument made in asphalt: this is the way, this is the shortest way, this is the way that makes sense if you value time above all else. A river is a negotiation. It goes around the hill because the hill is hard. It meanders because the soil is soft here and hard there, because a flood rearranged things a century ago and it is still adjusting. To follow a river on foot is to learn that a journey does not have to justify itself by its efficiency. The river arrives eventually, at the sea, which is the humblest and most final destination imaginable, and it arrives having taken a thousand detours that made it longer and more interesting and, in the end, more itself. I think about rivers whenever I am tempted to edit myself into a straight line for the sake of clarity.

Thinking, at least the kind I value most, is also river-like. It does not proceed in a neat chain of premises leading to a conclusion, though we pretend in essays and in arguments that it does, and we are often right to pretend, because clarity matters and other people need to follow us. But the actual experience of having an idea is usually messier than that. You are thinking about what to cook for dinner, and suddenly you remember a song you heard in a kitchen in 1998, and that song reminds you of the person who was singing it, and that person reminds you of a debt you never repaid, and that debt reminds you of the ethics of gratitude, and before you know it you are no longer thinking about dinner at all. You are somewhere else entirely, in a country you did not know was connected to your kitchen. To call this distraction is to miss the point. The dinner thought was the gate. The walk beyond the gate is the real thought.

Books have always been my favorite permitted form of wandering. A good library is a forest where you are allowed to cut across between trees that have nothing to do with each other. You go in looking for a book on the history of umbrellas and you come out with a book on the migrations of birds, because the bird book was next to the umbrella book on a shelf that had been arranged by someone with a sense of humor, and you followed a thread of curiosity that no catalog could have predicted. Novelists understand this. The best of them will let a character walk down a street for three pages, noticing the smell of rain on hot pavement and the particular quality of a stranger's laugh, long after the plot has technically been served. That walking is not filler. It is the texture of a mind paying attention to a world that exists for its own sake, not only to advance a story.

There is a pleasure in the tangent that efficiency cannot account for. I once spent an afternoon reading about the invention of the paperclip, not because I needed to know about paperclips, but because the phrase “invention of the paperclip” had appeared in a footnote somewhere and it lodged, unreasonably, in my mind like a burr. I learned about wire and about office work in the nineteenth century and about a Norwegian who patented a design that was not even his. Knowing this will never help me get to the airport faster. It will never help me file my taxes. It sits in my head like a small, polished stone I picked up on a walk and carried home for no reason except that it was interesting to hold. A mind, I suspect, is healthiest when it collects such stones, when it allows itself to be interested in things that have no immediate use, because use is a narrow category and interest is a wide one.

Music, especially when you listen to it while walking, is wandering made audible. A melody sets out from a home note and travels, visiting neighboring notes, sometimes going far away into a strange key, sometimes getting lost in a modulation that seems to have no way back, and then, miraculously, returning home, but home is not quite the same because you have been on the journey. I think of long instrumental pieces, of jazz solos that wander for eight minutes through a landscape of chords, of a folk song that can be sung at a kitchen table with no accompaniment and still carry you across a county. You do not listen to such music to arrive. You listen to it to be in motion. The arrival, when it comes, is a kind of grace, not a goal.

Conversation, when it is good, is also a form of shared wandering. Two people begin by talking about the weather, which is the polite map of talk, and then someone mentions a dream they had, and suddenly they are talking about childhood, and then about fear, and then about a book neither of them remembered reading until the other mentioned it. They have drifted far from the weather. They may never get back to it. That is not a failure of conversation. That is conversation doing its proper work, which is to discover what the two people actually care about, which is rarely the weather. The best talk I have ever had has felt like walking with a friend in a city neither of us knows, where we kept turning down side streets because they looked interesting, and we got thoroughly, happily lost, and we talked the whole way.

History, read generously, is full of wanderers who were not conquerors. We tend to celebrate the explorers who planted flags and drew lines and claimed continents, and perhaps we should, because we need to understand how the modern map was made, for better and for worse. But I am also drawn to the smaller wanderers, the ones who walked a coastline to see what was there, who collected plants, who learned words in a language that had no written form, who were curious in a way that was not immediately useful to an empire. Their curiosity produced knowledge that outlived the empires that tried to use it. Wandering, in that sense, is a radical act. It says that attention is valuable even when it cannot be taxed, that a person walking slowly through an unfamiliar place is not wasting time but gathering a kind of wealth that cannot be extracted or sold.

We live, now, in a culture that is suspicious of any journey that cannot be optimized. We have turned almost everything into a problem of arrival. We ask what a walk is for, what a book is for, what a conversation is for, as if the only valid answer were a measurable outcome. We measure our steps, our hours of sleep, our productivity, our streaks. We have apps that will nudge us back onto the path if we stray. We have turned the blue line into a moral authority. Turn left in two hundred feet. Do not stray. Do not waste. It is efficient, and I use it every day, and I am grateful for it, but I also notice, more and more, what it costs us. It costs us the accidental encounter, the unplanned view, the conversation with a stranger because we were both waiting for a bus that never came and decided to walk instead.

Digital wandering is the strange, compromised child of this culture. We scroll, and we call it wandering, but scrolling is usually not wandering at all. It is being herded. An algorithm has decided, with excellent statistics, what you are likely to look at next, and it is leading you down a path that is not chosen by you but for you, and the path is designed to keep you on it as long as possible, which is not the same as delightful. Real wandering requires friction. You have to push open a door. You have to get a little cold. You have to be in a place where the Wi-Fi does not work and you have to look up with your own eyes. The phone in my pocket can be a map, and a library, and a compass, and it can also be a leash. The difference is not the device. The difference is whether I remember that I am allowed to put it away and get lost on purpose.

Silence has a role in all of this that we undervalue. Wandering, whether on foot or in thought, often involves stretches where nothing much happens. You walk a long straight road with fields on both sides. You think a thought and then you think nothing for a while. You listen to a piece of music and there is a quiet passage where the instruments drop out and you are left with a single note hanging in the air. We are trained to fill those silences, to treat them as errors. But in my experience, the silences are where the wandering becomes integrated. They are the pauses that allow a mind to notice what it has gathered. Without them, you are just collecting impressions like a tourist collecting souvenirs. With them, you begin to understand what you actually saw.

Slowness, then, is not merely the absence of speed. It is a discipline, a way of paying attention that modern life makes difficult and therefore valuable. To walk slowly is to allow the world to present itself at a pace that the eye and the mind can actually absorb. To read slowly is to allow a sentence to finish its work before rushing to the next. To talk slowly is to allow a thought to become fully formed before it is spoken. I am not romantic about slowness for its own sake. I am impatient, like everyone else, and I want to get things done. But I have noticed that the things I remember most clearly, the things that have changed me most, almost always arrived slowly, through a side door, while I was not looking directly at them.

There is also the wandering we do with other people, which is different from wandering alone. Walking with a friend changes the geometry of attention. You point things out to each other. You notice what the other person notices, and your own noticing is altered by theirs. A street you have walked a hundred times becomes interesting again because you see it through a friend's habits of looking. A thought you have had a hundred times becomes new because you say it aloud to someone who has never heard it. I think this is why pilgrimages are rarely done entirely alone, and why even solitary wanderers write accounts of their journeys, as if to invite a companion along the route they have already traveled. We want our wandering to be witnessed, not to prove it happened, but to share the pleasure of having been somewhere.

And yet, wandering alone has its own irreplaceable gift, which is that it returns you to yourself. When you walk without a companion, there is no one to perform for, no one to impress with the cleverness of your observations. You can be bored. You can be sad. You can think a foolish thought and discard it without embarrassment. You can notice that you are tired, or hungry, or suddenly, inexplicably, happy, and all of that is allowed because no one is keeping score. I think a great deal of our modern anxiety comes from the feeling that we are always being observed, always on a stage, always being measured. Wandering alone, in a field or in a thought, is a way of stepping off that stage for a while.

What do we find when we wander? The honest answer is: often nothing that can be named. We find a new route home. We find a word we did not know we knew. We find that our knee hurts and that we need better shoes. We find that the light was beautiful and that we want to remember it. We find that we have been thinking about the same problem in the same way for years and that a change of scenery has loosened it, not solved it, but loosened it enough that we can see a different angle. Wandering rarely delivers a treasure. It delivers something more modest and more durable: a slightly altered attention, a slightly more forgiving attitude toward uncertainty, a reminder that we are creatures who move through time and space and that movement is not always in service of a purpose.

Perhaps that is why I return, again and again, to the image of a river. A river does not know where it is going in the sense of having a plan. It follows the slope of the land. It is shaped by what it encounters. It is both determined and flexible, both persistent and changeable. If I were to choose a patron saint for free writing, it would be a river. It would not set out to prove a point. It would set out to move, and in moving, it would carve a valley, and in the valley, other things would grow. The writing would meander. It would double back. It would linger where the soil is rich and hurry where the land is hard. And it would arrive, eventually, at a sea that is larger and quieter than any of its particulars.

So let this be that kind of writing. Let it have wandered. Let it have visited fields and maps and rivers and libraries and kitchen tables and quiet passages, and let it have returned, not to where it started exactly, but to a place nearby that looks different because of the journey. If you have followed it this far, you have also wandered, in the sense that you have spent time in the company of thoughts that were not assigned to you. You may not remember all of them. That is fine. Wandering is not about retention. It is about having been in motion in good company, even if the company was only a voice on a page and the motion was only the motion of reading.

And now, having arrived here, at what might be called an end, I find I do not want to conclude in the way that essays are supposed to conclude, with a summary and a moral neatly tied up. I want to leave a door open. I want to suggest that you, too, might go out for a walk without a destination, or open a book at random, or follow a tangent in a conversation and see where it leads, or listen to a piece of music all the way through without checking your phone. I want to suggest that the most valuable thing you can do with your attention today is to waste a little of it beautifully, on something that gives you no return except the pleasure of having noticed it. The field behind the house is still there, in my memory if not in fact. The grass is tall. The ditch is crooked. The circuit is waiting to be walked again, and it will not be the same circuit twice.

And now, having arrived here, at what might be called an end, I find I do not want to conclude in the way that essays are supposed to conclude, with a summary and a moral neatly tied up. I want to leave a door open. I want to suggest that you, too, might go out for a walk without a destination, or open a book at random, or follow a tangent in a conversation and see where it leads, or listen to a piece of music all the way through without checking your phone. I want to suggest that the most valuable thing you can do with your attention today is to waste a little of it beautifully, on something that gives you no return except the pleasure of having noticed it. The field behind the house is still there, in my memory if not in fact. The grass is tall. The ditch is crooked. The circuit is waiting to be walked again, and it will not be the same circuit twice.
